Lack of a predefined conceptual schema or organized data model

MP3 Audio

Solid-state memory registers

Historical biases in loan decisions may be learned and propagated by the model, discriminating against protected demographics
Relational databases cannot handle numerical floats
The model will require too much electrical power

The entitlement of individuals to obtain meaningful information about the logic involved in automated decisions affecting them
The requirement that all algorithms be programmed in C
The rule that companies must explain how they price products

A mathematical framework that allows querying aggregate datasets while guaranteeing that individual records cannot be identified
Deleting half of the database randomly
Using different passwords for different users

A relational database with only 10 tables

A Data Warehouse stores clean, curated, highly structured data with a predefined relational schema optimized for querying (schema-on-write)
A Data Warehouse is always cheaper than a Data Lake
Data Warehouses cannot connect to SQL tools

prompt: What is Data Governance?

The holistic framework of policies, processes, roles, and metrics that ensure effective and secure data management throughout an organization
The physical security guard patrolling a server room
Writing firmware for network routers

Personally Identifiable Information

prompt: What is the primary danger of 'Data Snooping' or 'P-Hacking' in data science research?

Repeatedly searching through data until an accidental statistically significant relationship is found, leading to false discoveries
It damages solid state drives
It makes plots appear in black and white

prompt: What is 'Concept Drift' in deployed machine learning systems?

The statistical degradation of model predictive accuracy over time due to changes in the underlying distribution and real-world relationships of target variables
The physical overheating of graphics processing units
Users forgetting their system login credentials

explanation: Concept drift occurs when the statistical properties of the target variable and its relationship to input features change over time in production.

A documented record tracing the origins, transformations, and movements of data across its lifecycle
The speed at which data travels through optical cables
The compression ratio of a zip file

The diverse structural forms of data, spanning tabular, audio, video, sensor signals, and text
The variety of colors used in dashboard charts
The different brands of server hardware

Veracity
Volatility
Voltage

The verified, empirical real-world target outcome (labels) against which model predictions are measured

Artificially generated data that mimics the statistical properties of real data without containing real individuals' private records
Faulty data corrupted by computer viruses
Data manually guessed by software developers

Principle of Maximum Profitability
Law of Diminishing Returns
Moore's Law

prompt: What is an 'Unbalanced Dataset' (or Class Imbalance) in classification problems?

options.text: A dataset where numerical floats do not sum to 100
A situation where one target class significantly outnumbers other classes (e.g., 99.9% non-fraud vs 0.1% fraud)
A CSV file with unequal column widths
A database distributed across unequal hard drive partitions

explanation: Class imbalance occurs when instances of one class dominate the training distribution, requiring specialized sampling techniques.

prompt: What is the primary role of a 'Data Dictionary' (Metadata Catalog)?

options.text: To translate Python code into spoken English
To provide standardized metadata descriptions including column definitions, data types, allowed values, and business rules
To list the names of all employees who have access to the office
To store dictionary objects in Python memory

prompt: In CRISP-DM, what is the output of the 'Data Preparation' phase?

The clean, transformed, feature-engineered dataset ready for consumption by machine learning algorithms
A printed invoice for client billing
The initial project charter document

prompt: Why is 'Reproducibility' considered a cornerstone of rigorous scientific data analysis?

options.text: It guarantees that cloud compute costs remain zero
It ensures that another researcher using the same data and analytical code can achieve identical empirical results
It prevents computers from crashing during training
It allows multiple developers to edit code simultaneously

prompt: What is 'Data Drift' as compared to 'Concept Drift'?

options.text: Data Drift occurs when input feature distributions P(X) change over time, even if the underlying conditional relationship P(Y|X) remains unchanged
Data Drift refers to hard drives drifting off their server mounts
Data Drift is an intentional feature of relational databases
There is no difference between Data Drift and Concept Drift

explanation: Data drift (covariate shift) refers to statistical shifts in the input feature space P(X), whereas concept drift refers to changes in the target relationship P(Y|X).

The physical weight of the server racks

A decentralized machine learning approach where models are trained locally on edge devices/servers without exchanging raw private user data
Teaching government officials how to code in Python
Connecting multiple SQL databases with standard foreign keys

Adobe Photoshop

Retrieving raw data from heterogeneous sources (databases, CRM, APIs, flat files) for staging
Permanently deleting redundant database indexes
Plotting line charts on an executive dashboard

prompt: What is the primary objective of data pre-processing in machine learning workflows?

options.text: To increase file sizes for cloud billing
To transform raw, noisy, incomplete real-world data into a clean, consistent format suitable for algorithm training
To compile Python scripts into binary machine code
To encrypt hard drive partitions

prompt: Which missing data mechanism describes a scenario where the probability of missingness depends entirely on observed variables and not the missing value itself?

options.text: Missing Completely at Random (MCAR)
Missing at Random (MAR)
Missing Not at Random (MNAR)
Deterministic Data Erasure

explanation: Missing at Random (MAR) means the propensity for a data point to be missing is related to other observed data, but not the missing data itself.

prompt: What does 'Missing Completely at Random' (MCAR) signify?

options.text: The missing values depend strongly on the unobserved variable itself
The probability of missingness is entirely independent of both observed and unobserved data
The entire column was dropped intentionally by the database administrator
The missing data occurs only on odd-numbered rows

explanation: Under MCAR, missingness is completely random and unbiased by any variable in the dataset.

prompt: Which technique handles missing numerical values by substituting the arithmetic mean of observed values?

options.text: Mean Imputation
Listwise Deletion
Hot-Deck Sampling
One-Hot Encoding

explanation: Mean imputation replaces missing values in a numerical column with the mean of available observations.

prompt: What is a major mathematical drawback of using Mean Imputation for missing values?

options.text: It changes the column data type to a string
It artificially reduces the variance of the variable and distorts covariance with other features
It causes infinite loops in CPU processing
It converts negative numbers into positive numbers

explanation: Mean imputation concentrates probability density at the mean, artificially deflating variance and attenuating standard errors.

prompt: What is 'Listwise Deletion' (Complete Case Analysis)?

options.text: Deleting the first ten rows of every table
Excluding any record (entire row) that has one or more missing values across analyzed variables
Removing the list data structure in Python memory
Renaming column headers to remove spaces

explanation: Listwise deletion discards every observation that contains at least one missing entry.

prompt: Under which condition can Listwise Deletion introduce severe bias into a model?

options.text: When data is Missing Completely at Random (MCAR)
When missingness is not random (MAR or MNAR), leading to systemic exclusion of specific population subgroups
When the dataset has fewer than 10 columns
When using a Linux operating system

explanation: If data is not MCAR, listwise deletion distorts the sample distribution, biasing model parameter estimates.

prompt: What is 'K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) Imputation'?

options.text: Imputing missing values using the average or mode of the K most similar data instances in the feature space
Replacing missing values with random numbers between 1 and K
Deleting K rows whenever a null is encountered
Assigning the alphabet letter K to missing cells

explanation: KNN imputation calculates Euclidean or Gower distances between instances to borrow values from the K nearest neighbors.

prompt: What is an 'Outlier' in statistical data analysis?

options.text: A data point that lies outside the boundary of the computer screen
An observation that deviates markedly from the overall pattern of distribution of the remaining data
A software engineer who works outside the office
A variable stored in an external file

explanation: An outlier is an extreme data point whose divergence from the rest of the sample suggests abnormal variation or measurement error.

prompt: In box plot analysis, an observation is considered an outlier if it falls below:

options.text: Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
Q1 + 1.5 * IQR
Median - 2 * IQR
Mean - Standard Deviation

explanation: Tukey's box plot rule identifies lower outliers as points falling below Q1 - 1.5 * IQR (where IQR = Q3 - Q1).

prompt: In box plot analysis, what defines an upper outlier?

options.text: A value greater than Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
A value greater than Q2 * 1.5
A value greater than Maximum * 2
A value equal to the mean

explanation: Tukey's rule defines upper outliers as observations exceeding Q3 + 1.5 * IQR.

prompt: What is the Z-Score of a data point x in a distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ?

options.text: Z = (x - μ) / σ
Z = (x + μ) * σ
Z = (x * σ) / μ
Z = σ / (x - μ)

explanation: The standard Z-score formula is Z = (x - mean) / standard_deviation.

prompt: In a standard normal distribution, observations with an absolute Z-Score exceeding which threshold are conventionally flagged as outliers?
explanation: In standard Gaussian distributions, 99.7% of data lies within 3 standard deviations; values with |Z| > 3 are rare and typically treated as outliers.

prompt: What is 'Winsorization' (or Capping) of outliers?

options.text: Deleting all outlier rows from the dataset permanently
Replacing extreme outlier values with the nearest non-outlier percentile limit (e.g., 1st or 99th percentile)
Converting outliers into imaginary numbers
Multiplying outliers by zero

explanation: Winsorizing caps extreme values at a designated percentile threshold rather than dropping the records entirely.

prompt: What is the formula for Min-Max Feature Scaling (Normalization) to rescale values into the interval [0, 1]?

options.text: x_scaled = (x - x_min) / (x_max - x_min)
x_scaled = (x - x_mean) / x_std
x_scaled = x * (x_max - x_min)
x_scaled = (x_max - x) / x_min

explanation: Min-Max Normalization rescales a feature to [0, 1] using (x - x_min) / (x_max - x_min).

prompt: What is the primary difference between Normalization (Min-Max) and Standardization (Z-score scaling)?

options.text: Normalization bounds data strictly between [0, 1], while Standardization centers data at mean 0 with unit variance without bounding the extremes
Normalization handles strings, while Standardization handles floats
Standardization eliminates all outliers automatically
There is no difference; they are identical formulas

explanation: Standardization centers features at mean 0 and standard deviation 1, accommodating outliers better than Min-Max scaling which compresses distribution ranges.

prompt: Why is feature scaling essential before training algorithms like K-Means Clustering and Support Vector Machines (SVM)?

options.text: Because these algorithms rely on geometric distance metrics (e.g., Euclidean distance) that are dominated by features with arbitrarily larger numerical ranges
Because Python cannot multiply unscaled numbers
Because scaling speeds up hard disk read operations
Because unscaled numbers cause syntax errors in compilers

explanation: Distance-based algorithms weigh attributes disproportionately if one feature has an order of magnitude larger scale (e.g., salary vs age).

prompt: Which machine learning models are inherently invariant to monotonic feature scaling?

options.text: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
Decision Trees and Random Forests
Support Vector Machines with RBF kernel
Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

explanation: Tree-based algorithms split nodes based on order inequalities and thresholds, making them completely invariant to monotonic numerical scaling.

prompt: What is 'One-Hot Encoding' in categorical feature preprocessing?

options.text: Converting categorical strings into a single running integer column (1, 2, 3...)
Creating a new binary (0 or 1) indicator column for each unique category in a categorical feature
Hashing the column values using MD5 checksums
Capitalizing all string characters

explanation: One-Hot Encoding transforms categorical levels into binary columns where exactly one bit is 'hot' (1) and all others are 0.

prompt: What critical mathematical problem arises if all N binary columns from One-Hot Encoding are included in a linear regression model with an intercept?

options.text: The Dummy Variable Trap (Perfect Multicollinearity)
Catastrophic Floating Point Overflow
Infinite Variance Inflation
Zero Division Error

explanation: The Dummy Variable Trap occurs because the sum of all dummy columns equals 1 (a linear combination of the intercept), causing multicollinearity; N-1 dummies must be used.

prompt: When should 'Ordinal Encoding' be preferred over 'One-Hot Encoding'?

options.text: When the categorical feature has no natural ordering (e.g., colors: Red, Blue, Green)
When the categorical feature possesses a distinct, meaningful inherent rank or hierarchy (e.g., Low, Medium, High)
When the dataset contains more than one million rows
When training deep neural networks exclusively

explanation: Ordinal encoding maps ordered levels to integers (e.g., Poor=0, Average=1, Excellent=2), preserving the ordinal relationships.

prompt: What is 'Target Encoding' (Mean Encoding)?

options.text: Replacing each categorical value with the average target variable value for that category
Replacing every feature with the target variable column directly
Sorting the dataset according to the target column
Deleting the target column before training

explanation: Target encoding maps each categorical level to the posterior expected value of the target variable within that category.

prompt: What is the primary risk associated with Target Encoding?

options.text: High computational latency during testing
Severe Target Leakage and Overfitting, especially for rare categorical levels
Creating negative numbers in positive distributions
Corrupting the database index schema

explanation: Target encoding directly exposes target information to feature columns; without cross-validation smoothing, it causes severe overfitting.

prompt: What is 'Data Integration' in the data preparation phase?

options.text: Combining data from multiple heterogeneous sources into a unified, coherent data store
Dividing a single CSV file into multiple small files
Encrypting database tables before transmission
Translating SQL queries into Java functions

explanation: Data integration reconciles disparate schemas, naming conventions, and data formats from multiple sources into a consistent consolidated store.

prompt: What is the 'Entity Identification Problem' in data integration?

options.text: Identifying which company manufactures a server
Recognizing that real-world entities are referred to by different identifiers across databases (e.g., 'Cust_ID' vs 'Client_Num')
Determining the MAC address of a network router
Locating the power button on an edge gateway

explanation: Entity identification matches real-world entities across disparate datasets where schemas, keys, or naming conventions differ.

prompt: What is 'Data Redundancy' in database integration?

options.text: Having zero backup copies of a database
The unnecessary duplication of data fields across multiple tables, which can cause update anomalies and inconsistency
Compressing tables using gzip algorithms
Running two queries in parallel

explanation: Redundancy occurs when the same attribute is stored in multiple locations, consuming unnecessary storage and risking inconsistency.

prompt: Which statistical test is used during data integration to detect correlation between categorical attributes and eliminate redundant features?

options.text: Chi-Square (χ²) Test of Independence
T-Test of Means
Euclidean Vector Metric
Mann-Whitney U Test

explanation: The Chi-Square test determines whether there is a statistically significant association between two categorical variables.

prompt: What is 'Data Transformation'?

options.text: Moving physical hard drives to another facility
The process of converting data from one format, structure, or scale into another suitable for analytical modeling
Deleting old log files automatically
Rewriting Python code into C++ code

explanation: Data transformation encompasses aggregation, scaling, normalization, attribute construction, and discretization.

prompt: What is 'Log Transformation' commonly used for in data preprocessing?

options.text: To convert numbers into Roman numerals
To stabilize variance, reduce positive (right) skewness, and make heavy-tailed distributions more Gaussian-like
To multiply all values by 10
To delete zero values

explanation: Taking the natural log (log(x) or log(1+x)) compresses extreme right-tail values, reducing skewness and conforming closer to normal assumptions.

prompt: What is the Box-Cox Transformation?

options.text: A physical packaging technique for hard disks
A parametric power transformation technique that transforms non-normal dependent variables into approximately normal shapes
A method for drawing 3D box plots
A technique for converting integers to booleans

explanation: Box-Cox finds an optimal power parameter λ to transform non-normal positive data into an approximately normal distribution.

prompt: What is 'Data Reduction' in data preprocessing?

options.text: Erasing half of the database to save cloud storage fees
Techniques that reduce the volume or dimensionality of a dataset while producing identical or substantially similar analytical results
Running algorithms at lower CPU frequencies
Reducing font sizes in terminal logs

explanation: Data reduction decreases representation size through dimensionality reduction, numerosity reduction, or compression without losing analytical fidelity.

prompt: What is 'Dimensionality Reduction'?

options.text: Reducing the physical dimensions of a server rack
The process of reducing the number of random variables (features/columns) under consideration in a dataset
Changing 3D plots into 2D plots
Limiting the number of users connected to a database

explanation: Dimensionality reduction condenses high-dimensional feature spaces into lower-dimensional representations while retaining essential information.

prompt: What is the 'Curse of Dimensionality'?

options.text: A computer hardware virus affecting high-end GPUs
